subtype: Approach: mock interviews with a peer for feedback [Action]
passage: Every Thursday after lectures, Nour and Beatriz pushed the sofa aside in their Lisbon flat. Nour asked, Beatriz answered, and a phone leaned against a stack of textbooks recorded it all. Then they played it back with a notebook. "You said 'basically' eleven times," Nour wrote. Beatriz laughed and groaned at once 😅. Her note for Nour was different: "The warehouse project goes from result to problem, which is confusing." They chose one fix each per week. Week one, cut 'basically'. Week two, start with the problem. By week four the recordings were shorter, and Beatriz's answers had a beginning, a middle and an end. Nour's next fix was eye contact.

qa.q: How many times did Nour count 'basically' in Beatriz's answer?
What did Beatriz feel when she heard her count of 'basically'?
qa.a: She felt amused and a little embarrassed, since she laughed and groaned at once. 😅

qa.q: What other approach could sit beside these sessions, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a careers adviser to sit in once, because a stranger's fresh ear catches habits two friends may have stopped noticing.

qa.q: What is it like for Nour to be part of these weekly sessions?
qa.a: Nour plays interviewer and gets feedback too, so Nour's own next fix, eye contact, comes from the same process of replaying and noting.

grounding: Shows two friends interviewing each other weekly, recording, noting filler words and unclear explanations, and fixing one weakness at a time.

subtype: Approach: mock interviews with a peer for feedback [Action]
passage: Every Wednesday at 5 pm, Akash and Himani booked the small discussion room in the college library. One interviewed, one answered, and a phone on the table recorded it all. Then they played it back with a notebook open. In week one, Himani counted Akash's "basically": nineteen times in ten minutes. He winced. "Fine. This week's fix: no basically." In week two, the count was four. But the recording showed another problem: when Himani asked about his internship, he explained the tools, not what the project did. Week three's fix: start every answer with the problem, then the solution. Himani's own recordings showed her talking too fast when nervous; her fix was one breath before each answer. By week five, a senior listened to old and new recordings and said they both sounded like different people. Akash grinned. "Better people, I hope."

qa.q: How many times did Akash say basically in week one?
How did Akash feel on hearing the count?
qa.a: Akash felt embarrassed, wincing at the number, but determined enough to make it that week's fix.

qa.q: What else could the pair try as they improve?
qa.a: They could invite a third person to ask unexpected questions, so they practise thinking on their feet, not only polishing answers.

qa.q: How might Himani experience the mock sessions?
qa.a: Himani gets honest feedback on her own fast talking and a steady partner, so both of them improve, not just Akash.

grounding: Shows two friends interviewing each other weekly, recording answers, noting filler words and unclear parts, and fixing one weakness each week.

subtype: Approach: mock interviews with a peer for feedback [Action]
passage:
Subject: weekly mock interviews? (please say yes)
Hi Sarita,
After my interview on Monday, I played back the practice recording I'd made on my phone the night before, and finally heard what the panel heard. I say "like" in every sentence, and when I explain my final-year project I start with the software and never say what problem it solves.
Here's my idea. Every Saturday at 10, one hour, in the reading room or on video. We take turns interviewing each other and record it. Afterwards we each write down the filler words and the most confusing part.
Then we pick ONE thing to fix for the next week. Only one. Otherwise I'll try to fix everything and fix nothing.
I'll bring a list of questions. You bring your project explanation, since you said yours feels messy too.
Tell me if Saturday works.
Usha

qa.a: Every Saturday at 10, for one hour.

qa.q: How did Usha feel listening to the recording?
qa.a: Usha felt uncomfortable but clearer, finally hearing the filler words and muddled explanation the panel heard.

qa.q: What else could make the mock interviews more useful?
qa.a: They could each keep a short log of the weekly fix and play an old recording after a month to hear real progress.

qa.q: How might Sarita see the invitation?
qa.a: Sarita, whose project explanation also feels messy, may welcome a regular partner and a clear one-fix-a-week plan.

grounding: Illustrates a student proposing weekly recorded mock interviews with a friend, noting filler words and unclear answers and fixing one thing a week.
